title: Neural Quantum States in Mixed Precision
claim: Theoretical error bounds on perturbed MCMC acceptance hold empirically, and perturbation effects stay small until noise exceeds a threshold.
layout: 3 panels in a row, left-to-right, shared colorbars, log-scale axes
description: Three side-by-side scientific plots. Panel (a) is a heatmap on log-scaled x-axis s(x,y) from 1e-4 to 1e2 and y-axis ε(x,y) from 0 to 3, with a viridis colorbar for |Δα(x,y)|. A red line marks s = e^{-ε}, with a vertical dashed red line at s=1 and thin contour lines. Panel (b) is a log-log scatter of relative error ε_rel against noise σ. Blue and green points mark two observables, ⟨Π_Even⟩ and ⟨σ^x⟩. A dashed purple KL bound and a dashed red average bound are overlaid, with a shaded green confidence region. Panel (c) plots α−α̃ against σ on a log x-axis. Many curves are colored by h/J with a viridis colorbar. A thick black bound curve rises sigmoidally, and dashed horizontal lines mark the unperturbed acceptance rates. The eye goes first to the colorful heatmap and the red bound lines.
caption: Panel (a) displays the acceptance difference |∆α(x, y)| as a function of the acceptance ratio s(x, y) and the error difference ε(x, y). The solid red line corresponds to s(x, y) = e−ε(x,y). For ε(x, y) < 0 the plot is inverted over both the x-axis and y-axis. Panels (b) and (c) present results for the noisy RBM. Panel (b) shows the relative error between expectation values computed with the unperturbed and noisy RBM as a function of noise parameter σ compared to the KL bound of Eq. 8 and the average bound of Eq. 13. The expected values of both the Pauli-X operator σx and the projector onto the even bitstrings ΠEven are investigated. abstract: Scientific computing has long relied on double precision (64-bit floating point) arithmetic to guarantee accuracy in simulations of real-world phenomena. However, the growing availability of hardware accelerators such as Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) has made low-precision formats attractive due to their superior performance, reduced memory footprint, and improved energy efficiency. In this work, we investigate the role of mixed-precision arithmetic in neural-network based Variational Monte Carlo (VMC), a widely used method for solving computationally otherwise intractable quantum many-body systems. We first derive general analytical bounds on the error introduced by reduced precision on Metropolis-Hastings MCMC, and then empirically validate these bounds on the use-case of VMC. We demonstrate that significant portions of the algorithm, in particular, sampling the quantum state, can be executed in half precision without loss of accuracy. More broadly, this work provides a theoretical framework to assess the applicability of mixed-precision arithmetic in machine-learning approaches that rely on MCMC sampling. In the context of VMC, we additionally demonstrate the practical effectiveness of mixed-precision strategies, enabling more scalable and energy-efficient simulations of quantum many-body systems.
